content:
Sleep disturbance affects up to 80% of people with arthritis. Pain, stiffness, and discomfort can make falling asleep difficult and staying asleep even harder. Yet good sleep is essential for managing arthritis — poor sleep increases pain sensitivity and inflammation.

Quick answer: To sleep better with arthritis, adjust your sleep position, use a medium-firm mattress, and consider a supportive pillow. For knee arthritis, place a pillow between or under your knees. For hip arthritis, sleep on your non-affected side with a pillow between knees. Timing pain medication to be effective at night, maintaining good sleep hygiene, and relaxing before bed can also help.

Why Arthritis Disrupts Sleep

  • Night-time pain — inflammatory cytokines peak during the night, increasing pain
  • Morning stiffness — joints stiffen overnight, causing discomfort that wakes you
  • Difficulty finding comfortable positions
  • Medication side effects — steroids can cause insomnia
  • Anxiety and low mood — common with chronic pain conditions

Sleep Position Tips

For Knee Arthritis

Place a pillow between your knees when sleeping on your side, or under your knees when on your back. This maintains alignment and reduces pressure.

For Hip Arthritis

Sleep on the non-affected side with a pillow between your knees. A mattress topper can help distribute pressure more evenly.

For Back Arthritis

Sleep on your back with a pillow under your knees, or on your side in a foetal position with a pillow between your knees.

For Shoulder Arthritis

Avoid sleeping on the affected shoulder. Hug a pillow to support the arm in a comfortable position.

Mattress and Pillow Choices

  • Medium-firm mattress — provides support without creating pressure points
  • Memory foam topper — moulds to your body shape (£30-80 from Argos, Dunelm)
  • Supportive pillow — memory foam or contoured pillows maintain neck alignment
  • V-shaped pillow — useful for propping up and supporting multiple joints

Pain Relief Timing

Speak to your GP about timing your pain medication so it's most effective during the night. Slow-release anti-inflammatories taken at bedtime can help some people.

Sleep Hygiene for Arthritis

  • Keep a consistent bedtime and wake time
  • Take a warm bath or shower before bed — heat relaxes muscles and eases stiffness
  • Keep bedroom temperature at 16-18°C
  • Avoid screens for 30 minutes before bed
  • Try relaxation techniques — the NHS Couch to 5K app includes sleep stories

When to Get Help

If sleep problems persist despite these measures, speak to your GP. The NHS offers:

  • CBT for insomnia (CBT-i) — available through NHS Talking Therapies
  • Sleep clinics — specialist assessment for complex sleep problems
  • Pain management programmes — multidisciplinary approach to chronic pain

Good sleep is a vital part of arthritis management. Don't accept poor sleep as inevitable — help is available through the NHS.

Practical next steps for How to Sleep Better with Arthritis

If you came here about How to Sleep Better with Arthritis, pick one change you can keep for a fortnight rather than overhauling everything at once. Note what hurts, what helps, and what you have already tried, then take that list to your GP, rheumatology nurse or physiotherapist so the conversation stays concrete.

In many areas you can ask your primary care network about self-referral to physiotherapy or lifestyle support without waiting for a hospital letter. Check your GP surgery website or the NHS App for the route that applies where you live.

Gentle cognitive tools

Noticing catastrophic thoughts ("this flare will never end") and reframing them with paced facts can reduce fear without denying real pain. Apps and courses based on cognitive behavioural approaches are available on the NHS in many areas; your surgery can advise what is offered locally.

Reliable UK sources

Cross-check major decisions with NHS.uk, your clinical team, and NICE guidance summaries where relevant. Be wary of social posts that promise reversal of arthritis or attack standard medicines without evidence.

Quick questions about Sleep Better with Arthritis

Is this a substitute for seeing a clinician? No. Use it to prepare questions and understand options, then confirm decisions with your NHS team.

How long before I judge whether a change helped? Give most habit or exercise changes at least two to four weeks, unless pain or swelling clearly worsens — in that case scale back sooner.

What should I track? Joint pain (0–10), morning stiffness time, sleep quality, and how far you can walk or how long you can type or stand. Patterns beat one-off ratings.

Safety and when to get urgent help

This page is general information for people in the United Kingdom, not personal medical advice. Seek urgent help via NHS 111 or A&E if you have sudden inability to move a joint, hot swollen joint with fever, chest pain, severe shortness of breath, or symptoms that feel immediately dangerous.

Keep expectations kind while you work on how to sleep better with arthritis. Arthritis symptoms fluctuate; a quieter week does not mean you imagined earlier pain, and a flare does not mean every helpful habit has failed. Adjust one variable at a time so you can see what truly helps.
